newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CHRISTMAS MEANS CARNAGE ON S.AFRICAN ROADS.
newsitem.headline: CHRISTMAS MEANS CARNAGE ON S.AFRICAN ROADS.

text.p: Christmas holidays in South Africa mean sun, family -- and one of the world's most appalling road death tolls, due largely to the odd mix of first and third worlds.
The National Traffic Information Centre said on Thursday 456 people had died on the roads since the holiday season officially began on December 3, with the busiest period still to come.
"We have the worst road safety statistics," said Bjorn van Oort, spokesman for the Automobile Association of South Africa.
"South Africa does not rate very well in terms of the number of people dying per 100 million kilometres."
Last December saw the highest monthly death toll for many years with 880 people killed as people abandon the populous Johannesburg area for distant coast resorts.
Road safety officials are running a major publicity drive to try and stop a grim new record being set this year in South Africa, which has some 40 million people but low private car ownership.
Many who die are pedestrians trying to dart across four-lane highways where BMWs, Mercedes and overcrowded minibus taxis race along, often ignoring the 120 kph (72 mph) speed limit.
"We have beautiful highways and freeways that enable us to travel at first-world speeds," van Oort said.

"Pedestrians frequently try to cross the road with vehicles travelling at 120 km per hour. The speeds travelled in the rest of Africa are much lower," he said. "Forty-three percent of people dying in collisions are pedestrians."

South Africa, with poor public transport, has a bad drink-driving problem but drink-walking is also a major cause of accidents, said National Traffic Information Centre spokeswoman Christa van De Walt.
"Drunken pedestrians are a hazard on the roads," she said.
Adding to the problem is the variety of wheels using main roads, from bicycles and barely roadworthy old wrecks to packed and overloaded taxi-buses and the fast foreign cars of the rich.
Speeding and reckless driving plague a country where many people behind the steering wheel have no driving licence.
"(Many) accidents are caused by impatience, overtaking on the barrier line, fatigue and lack of concentration," said van der Walt.
The statistics are horrific in terms of lives lost, but the economic cost to the country is equally shocking.
Van Oort said studies showed showed road accidents cost South Africa 10 billion rands ($2.13 billion) per year.
"This is a huge loss to any economy and especially one as fragile as South Africa's," van Oort said.
"We have this slaughter on the roads and every year information is handed out to road users. Only with a change in attitude, training and education can we really make a difference."
